sources.title: Wilhelm Röntgen (English Wikipedia) -- orientation only; not used as support for any scored row. Korean Wikipedia title '빌헬름 콘라트 뢴트겐' confirmed via the Wikidata kowiki sitelink.

Wilhelm Röntgen (Q35149) -- verified live via wbgetentities (2026-10-03): en label 'Wilhelm Röntgen', description 'German physicist (1845–1923)', de label 'Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen' ('deutscher Physiker und Nobelpreisträger'), ko label '빌헬름 콘라트 뢴트겐', P569 1845-03-27, P570 1923-02-10, P18 'Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen (1888-1900), 88374 p.jpg', enwiki 'Wilhelm Röntgen', kowiki '빌헬름 콘라트 뢴트겐', dewiki 'Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen'. Orientation only.

Otto Glasser, Dr. W. C. Röntgen (Springfield, Ill.: Charles C Thomas, 1945; 50th-anniversary condensation of his 1931/1934 biography 'Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen and the Early History of the Roentgen Rays', plus later letters and documents), archive.org Digital Library of India OCR text (in.ernet.dli.2015.63841), read: ch. I (schooling, Utrecht expulsion, Zurich), ch. II (Kundt years, Strassburg/Hohenheim/Giessen, 1888 Röntgen current, declined Jena/Utrecht calls, Würzburg rectorship 1894, Freiburg call declined), ch. III (8 Nov. 1895 discovery and the weeks of solitary work), ch. V (Jan.-March 1896: reprints sent 1 Jan., press storm, letter to Zehnder, Berlin demonstration, refusal of lecture invitations incl. the Reichstag, the single Würzburg lecture of 23 Jan. 1896), ch. VII in part (Sorrento retreat, AEG/Max Levy patent reply), ch. IX (1897-1923: teaching, publication habits, Lenard dispute, refused calls, Nobel 1901, 1905 congress, 1912 Laue diffraction reaction, wartime, will), and the chronology -- SCHOLAR/BIOGRAPHER (radiation physicist and historian of radiology; Glasser was a pupil of Röntgen's former Munich assistant Walter Friedrich and built the book from Röntgen's surviving letters, the Boveri family and Zehnder correspondence); admiring commemorative volume sponsored by radiological societies, with some narrative reconstruction ('one can only imagine') that is NOT used. Health, bereavement, childlessness, adoption and inflation-loss passages were read and are NOT used for any row.

H. J. W. Dam, 'The New Marvel in Photography: A Visit to Professor Röntgen at His Laboratory in Würzburg -- His Own Account of His Great Discovery', McClure's Magazine vol. 6 no. 5 (April 1896), pp. 403-415, archive.org OCR text (sim_new-mcclures-magazine_mcclures-magazine_1896-04_6_5), the Röntgen article read in full (the following 'Röntgen Rays in America' feature was not used) -- JOURNALIST, FIRSTHAND (an interview at the Würzburg institute in Jan./Feb. 1896, with Röntgen's answers quoted directly). Read: his self-built tin-box darkroom; his declining to say what the rays were ('I don't know'); 'I did not think; I investigated'; 'I am not a prophet, and I am opposed to prophesying ... as fast as my results are verified I shall make them public'; 'When I have done it, I will tell you'; refusing a portrait or photograph ('No, that is nonsense'; 'I am too busy'); impatience with personal questions; 'There is much to do, and I am busy, very busy'. Dam makes factual errors about Röntgen's life (says he was born near Zurich and took his degree at Utrecht) and writes in a breathless popular style, so only the directly quoted exchanges and observed behaviour are used, at moderate weight.

W. C. Röntgen, 'On a New Kind of Rays' (first communication, Würzburg, end of 1895), second communication (9 March 1896) and 'Further Observations on the Properties of the X-Rays' (third communication, 10 March 1897), English translation in G. F. Barker (ed.), Röntgen Rays: Memoirs by Röntgen, Stokes, and J. J. Thomson, Harper's Scientific Memoirs III (New York: Harper, 1899), pp. 1-40, archive.org OCR (rontgenraysmemoir00ront, Getty Research Institute copy) -- SELF. Read the first communication in full and the second and third in part. Read: the naming footnote ('For brevity's sake I shall use the expression "rays"; and to distinguish them from others of this name I shall call them "X-rays"'); 'wherever it has been possible ... I have controlled, by means of photography, every important observation which I have made with the eye'; 'I have tried in many ways to detect interference phenomena of the X-rays; but, unfortunately, without success'; experiments 'begun, but ... not yet finished'; his reasons for rejecting the ultraviolet hypothesis and his tentative longitudinal-ether-wave suggestion; second communication: 'I have, however, delayed the publication of my experiments until I could contribute results which are free from criticism'; third communication's control experiments (lead cylinder closed by 'the head of the observer'). Barker's preface (non-self editor, 1899) notes Lenard's prior observations and credits Röntgen with 'the first systematic study' -- used only as context.

Alexi Assmus, 'Early History of X Rays', Beam Line (SLAC) vol. 25 no. 2 (Summer 1995), pp. 10-24, PDF from slac.stanford.edu read in full (text extracted locally) -- SCHOLAR (historian of physics; independent of the Röntgen-family/radiology-society tradition). Read: that after noticing the fluorescing screen the newly elected Rector 'spent the next six weeks in his laboratory, working alone, and sharing nothing with his colleagues'; that he 'refused the calls' from Giessen until Würzburg offered its institute; his 1894 rectorial address; 'an exact experimenter who often made his own apparatus' and could measure extremely small effects; the obvious tests he ran on the new rays (rectilinear propagation, refraction, reflection, magnetic deflection) and his tentative longitudinal-wave suggestion; that he published only three papers on X rays; that at Munich, in negotiations over the Reichsanstalt offer, he obtained a second institute for theoretical physics in return for staying, which went to Sommerfeld. Assmus misdates the society 'delivery' (the paper was submitted, not read, on 28 Dec. 1895); used for the dated facts above, and for the wider history of the rays' nature only as context.

Nobel Prize in Physics 1901: presentation speech by C. T. Odhner (10 Dec. 1901) and the Nobel Foundation's biographical note on Röntgen (from Nobel Lectures, Physics 1901-1921, Elsevier 1967), nobelprize.org, both read in full -- INSTITUTIONAL. Used for achievement facts (prize 'for the discovery with which his name is linked for all time ... the so-called Röntgen rays or, as he himself called them, X-rays'; career dates; declined calls to Jena 1886, Utrecht 1888, Leipzig 1899, the Reichsanstalt presidency and the Berlin Academy chair). Its general characterisation ('strikingly modest and reticent', 'always shy of having an assistant, and preferred to work alone', 'much of the apparatus he used was built by himself') is an unattributed editorial summary and is used only as corroborating context, never as the main support of a row. The note's health/cause-of-death and adoption sentences are not used.

Jean-François Monville and Robert F. Dondelinger, 'Father and Son Jointly Announced the Discovery of Röntgen Rays in Two Consecutive Press Articles -- Revisited', Journal of the Belgian Society of Radiology 107(1):3 (2023), CC BY 4.0, full text via Europe PMC (PMC9818045), read in full -- SCHOLARS (radiologist-historians; independent, source-critical study of the Vienna press leak). Read: Röntgen mailed his offprint and prints no earlier than 1 Jan. 1896 to a selection of physicists (Stokes and Warburg acknowledged receipt on 3 Jan.); in a letter to Kohlrausch of 15 Jan. 1896 (Deutsches Röntgen-Museum holdings, as cited) he explained he could send prints at first only to Warburg and Exner and that he had had to do it all on his own because his assistant was away for the Christmas vacation; the authors find no evidence he disclosed the discovery to Exner before the paper; the Presse articles were written by the editor Lecher and his physicist son, not by Röntgen. Used for the dated mailing facts and his self-reliant handling of it; the Lecher reconstruction is context only.

Röntgen-Gedächtnisstätte Würzburg (memorial in the former Physical Institute, run by a Würzburg board of trustees), biography page 'Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen', wilhelmconradroentgen.de, read in full 2026-10-03 (German) -- INSTITUTIONAL. Read: that he named the rays 'X-Strahlen'; the 23 Jan. 1896 public talk at the invitation of the Physical-Medical Society and Kölliker's proposal of the name 'Röntgenstrahlen'; 'Röntgen lehnte es ab, sein Verfahren patentieren zu lassen'; that he gave the entire Nobel prize money (50,000 kronor) to the University of Würzburg for scientific research. Used only as independent institutional corroboration of these facts (alongside Glasser), never as sole support of a row.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_rontgen_memoirs_1896, src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_dam_1896, src_rontgen_assmus_1995 | Nov. 1895-1897 | self + biographer (with Röntgen's letters) + journalist (firsthand) + historian] Verification before claims, from several sides. His first communication states that 'wherever it has been possible ... I have controlled, by means of photography, every important observation which I have made with the eye', and lists the negative results (no refraction, no regular reflection, no interference found) rather than glossing them; the second (March 1896) says he had delayed publishing the discharge experiments 'until I could contribute results which are free from criticism' (self). Glasser documents that after 8 Nov. 1895 he worked in seclusion to convince himself before telling anyone, answering his friend Boveri, 'I have discovered something interesting, but I do not know whether or not my observations are correct', and in a Jan. 1896 letter to Zehnder (quoted) declined to adopt a speculative explanation: 'The facts are the important thing'. Dam, interviewing him in early 1896, recorded 'I did not think; I investigated' and 'as fast as my results are verified I shall make them public'. Assmus (independent historian) describes him running 'the obvious tests' -- rectilinear propagation, refraction, reflection, magnetic deflection -- before concluding the rays were not cathode rays. Held at 80/0.70 because the non-self accounts are mostly admiring.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_memoirs_1896 | 1888-1920s | biographer + self (letter and paper)] A high personal standard that delayed or prevented publication. In a letter to Hertz of 1 March 1888 (quoted by Glasser) he wrote 'I sometimes become impatient with my own experiments and must then begin all over again. I must postpone detailed publications of them'. Glasser states that only with great effort could he force himself to write up observations, that after the three X-ray communications he published nothing for years because his wish to investigate a subject 'most thoroughly' led to repeated revision, and that 'many important results he failed to publish because he feared the possible chance of an experimental error'. His own second communication holds back results until they are 'free from criticism'. dual_edged: the same standard made his three X-ray papers models of reliability but left work unpublished. Mostly one biographer plus self, so strong_inference at 0.60.

deep_focus.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_assmus_1995, src_rontgen_dam_1896 | 1888-1896 | biographer + historian + journalist + Röntgen's and his wife's letters as quoted] After 8 Nov. 1895 he set aside his rectorial and teaching routine and, in Assmus's words, 'spent the next six weeks in his laboratory, working alone'; Glasser adds that he devoted himself 'exclusively' to the new effect and returned to the laboratory the next morning to repeat the observations. When the press storm broke he complained to Zehnder (letter quoted by Glasser) that 'for exactly four weeks I was unable to make a single experiment', refused lecture invitations, including one from the Reichstag, 'in order that he might continue his own experiments', and declined further invitations in Munich and Rome in March 1896. In 1888 he declined the Utrecht chair because moving 'would require too much of my time, which I had rather devote to scientific investigations' (letter quoted by Glasser). Dam saw him end their interview with 'There is much to do, and I am busy, very busy', his eyes already on the inner laboratory, and his wife's letter of 4 March 1896 (quoted) records that he kept his thoughts on his work despite constant interruptions. Glasser's more dramatic details (eating and sleeping in the laboratory) are not relied on. Below 85 because the sustained-attention evidence centres on one exceptional period.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_assmus_1995 | 1870s-1896 | biographer + historian + Röntgen's lecture as reported] Two independent writers describe the same working trait: Glasser says he 'developed a skill for measuring very small physical effects with extreme accuracy' and that with Kundt he measured the electromagnetic rotation of the plane of polarisation in gases quantitatively, an effect Faraday had failed to demonstrate; Assmus, independently, calls him 'an exact experimenter' able 'to measure extremely small effects, surpassing even Faraday's measurement of the rotation of polarized light in gases'. A concrete instance from his own 23 Jan. 1896 lecture (as reported by Glasser): unexplained light strips on a plate exposed through a laboratory door led him to have the door dismantled, finding that its white-lead coat absorbed differently depending on the rays' direction. The Prussian Academy's 1919 address (quoted by Glasser) praises his 'keen, critical, and precise workmanship'. Admiring sources, one concrete self-reported episode; kept at 72/0.60.

social_assertiveness.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_dam_1896, src_rontgen_nobel | 1896-1905 | biographer + journalist (firsthand) + institutional note] Repeatedly declined to put himself forward. In 1896 he refused lecture invitations from the Reichstag and numerous scientific societies, and on the way to Italy declined invitations in Munich and from Salvioni and Righi in Rome; the Würzburg talk of 23 Jan. 1896, given only after an urgent request from colleagues, 'probably was the only one on the discovery that Röntgen ever gave before a large audience' (Glasser). He declined to give a Nobel lecture in 1901 and refused to attend the 1905 Berlin congress bearing his name, writing to Zehnder that he could not understand 'how my friends could do such a thing to me' (Glasser). Dam, in person, found him giving personal details only 'under good-natured protest', laughing at the idea of being famous and refusing a portrait or photograph ('No, that is nonsense'; 'I am too busy'). The Nobel note and Glasser both describe reticence with strangers. Counter-signals kept in view: he did lecture in Würzburg when asked, demonstrated before the Kaiser, and Glasser says he could be 'gruff and even rude' with self-important people. dual_edged: it protected his research time but left public explanation of his work to others.

collaboration.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_monville_2023, src_rontgen_nobel, src_rontgen_assmus_1995 | 1870-1906 | biographer + scholars + institutional note] Mostly solitary research with some genuine partnerships. Glasser says he was working alone on 8 Nov. 1895 'as was his custom and preference' and that his working habits kept him from confiding in his assistants during the discovery; in a letter of 15 Jan. 1896 to Kohlrausch (cited by Monville and Dondelinger) he explained he had had to prepare and send the first prints entirely on his own. The Nobel note says he was 'always shy of having an assistant, and preferred to work alone'. Against this, Glasser documents co-authored work: four papers with Kundt on magneto-optic rotation in gases, work with Exner on solar radiation, with Schneider on compressibility, with Zehnder on refraction under pressure and later with Joffe on crystals; Assmus notes he secured a theoretical-physics chair for Sommerfeld at Munich. Below the midpoint, not extreme.

curiosity.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_assmus_1995, src_rontgen_dam_1896 | 1870s-1895 | biographer + historian + Röntgen in interview] Wide-ranging inquiry and a mid-career move into an unfamiliar area. Glasser lists work on specific heats of gases, heat conduction and piezoelectricity in crystals, heat absorption by water vapour (an open Tyndall-Magnus dispute), compressibility of liquids, oil films on water and molecular size, and says he kept up with the literature by reading late into the night. In 1894-95, at almost fifty, he obtained a Lenard tube, repeated Lenard's experiments and dropped his dielectric-constant studies to work on cathode rays (Glasser); Assmus independently notes this line of work was 'outside Röntgen's usual research pursuits'. Röntgen himself told Dam he had long been interested in cathode rays and 'determined, as soon as I had the time, to make some researches of my own'. Breadth is within physics, and the evidence is descriptive rather than a single decisive episode, hence strong_inference at 0.56.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_rontgen_memoirs_1896, src_rontgen_glasser_1945 | 1895-1912 | self + editor's preface + biographer] Two documented revisions of his own view. In the first communication he tentatively proposed that the rays were longitudinal ether vibrations; G. F. Barker's 1899 preface to the English edition records that he 'at first was favorably inclined' to that idea 'but later he was convinced that they were essentially identical with light waves'. In 1912, when Friedrich showed him the Laue-Friedrich-Knipping diffraction photographs, Glasser reports that he examined them 'thoroughly and critically', found no experimental error but said 'I do not think that these are interference phenomena, they look different to me', and 'soon thereafter' became convinced they were. Initial caution followed by acceptance once the evidence stood; only two episodes, one source for the second, hence 0.52.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_rontgen_dam_1896, src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_assmus_1995, src_rontgen_nobel | 1870s-1896 | journalist (firsthand) + biographer + historian + institutional note] He improvised his own apparatus in modestly equipped laboratories. Dam was shown a self-made portable darkroom -- a tin box about seven feet high with an aluminium window placed against the tube -- and described the laboratory as 'bare and unassuming' compared with British and American ones. Glasser records a 'simple homemade but very sensitive air thermometer' used at Giessen to show that water vapour absorbs heat radiation, numerous self-built lecture-demonstration devices, and early posts in 'meagerly equipped' institutes; Assmus independently describes 'an exact experimenter who often made his own apparatus', and the Nobel note says much of his apparatus 'was built by himself'. Several instances from separate sources; held at 68 because the instances are small-scale.

persistence.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_nobel, src_rontgen_assmus_1995 | 1862-1874 | biographer + institutional note + historian] Kept going through repeated blocks to an academic career. Expelled from the Utrecht technical school after refusing to name the classmate who drew a caricature (Glasser; the Nobel note says 'unfairly expelled'), he spent almost a year preparing for a private matriculation examination, failed it before a hostile substitute examiner, audited Utrecht lectures, and then entered the Zurich Polytechnic by a route that did not require the usual credentials (Glasser; Assmus and the Nobel note confirm the Zurich route). At Würzburg in 1870-72 his lack of classical credentials again barred him from becoming a Privatdozent; after following Kundt to Strassburg he qualified there in 1874 'after two years of conscientious and hard work' (Glasser). Largely one biographer's narrative for the details, hence a moderate score.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_assmus_1995 | 1865-1906 | biographer + historian] Created conditions for his own and others' work rather than waiting. In 1865, dissatisfied with auditing at Utrecht, he applied 'at once' to the Zurich Polytechnic, writing 'Not satisfied with my course of studies at this university, I would like to follow the call of the Zurich school' (application quoted by Glasser). At Giessen he set out with his assistants to improve the poor facilities, and a new physics laboratory and lecture room were built in 1880 (Glasser). At Munich, in negotiations over the Reichsanstalt offer, he obtained a second institute for theoretical physics in return for staying (Assmus), which Glasser says was established for Sommerfeld 'at Röntgen's insistence' in 1906. Three episodes across two sources; outcomes partly depended on ministries and colleagues, so kept moderate.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_rontgen_glasser_1945, src_rontgen_gedaechtnisstaette | 1896-1901 | biographer + institutional memorial] Two documented decisions to give up control or reward so that the discovery and science would benefit others. When Max Levy of the AEG approached him about his firm's interest in developing the rays, he replied (as quoted by Glasser) that university discoveries 'belong to humanity and ... should not in any way be hampered by patents, licenses, contracts, nor should they be controlled by any one group'; the Würzburg Röntgen memorial independently states that he declined to patent the process. In 1901 he gave the Nobel prize money to the University of Würzburg for scientific purposes (Glasser; the memorial says the entire 50,000 kronor). Counter-signal: he did not pursue medical applications himself, offering instead to advise anyone who did (Glasser, Jan. 1896). The decisions are clear, but the motive is inferred from one quoted reply, so the score stays modest at 0.50.

Röntgen (1945) -- chapters I, II, III, V and IX and the chronology read, chapter VII in part (the 1934 Glasser biography with Margret Boveri's reminiscences is archive.org lending-only, HTTP 401, not read); Röntgen's three communications in the 1899 Harper's English edition (first in full, second and third in part) with Barker's preface; H. J. W. Dam's McClure's interview (April 1896) in full; Alexi Assmus, 'Early History of X Rays' (SLAC Beam Line 1995) in full; Monville and Dondelinger (J Belg Soc Radiol 2023) in full; the Nobel presentation speech and biographical note; the Röntgen-Gedächtnisstätte Würzburg biography page. Also skimmed and not used: the 2020 Insights into Imaging article on the prints Röntgen sent to Lorentz (PMC7054508; no behavioural content beyond the mailing). NOT READ / NOT AVAILABLE: Glasser 1934 (lending-only), Zehnder's 'Röntgens Briefe an L. Zehnder' (1935) and Joffe's recollections (not found in open full text), Nitske's 1971 biography -- so Röntgen's letters are used only as Glasser quotes them. INDEPENDENT PERSPECTIVES: (1) Röntgen himself -- the three communications, and his letters/speeches as quoted by Glasser -- ONE self perspective, never the sole support of a row; (2) Otto Glasser, biographer and radiation physicist, building on the Boveri and Zehnder correspondence (admiring commemorative volume sponsored by radiological societies; some narrative reconstruction not used); (3) H. J. W. Dam, journalist who interviewed and observed him in Würzburg in early 1896 (firsthand, error-prone on biography); (4) Alexi Assmus, historian of physics (1995, independent); (5) Monville and Dondelinger, radiologist-historians (2023, source-critical, independent); (6) institutional: Nobel Foundation texts and the Würzburg Röntgen memorial (achievement/fact corroboration only); G. F. Barker's 1899 editor's preface (non-self, contemporary) used once in belief_updating. NON-SELF behavioural sources: Glasser (secret verification period, lecture refusals, patent reply, prize donation, Nobel lecture and 1905 congress refusals, publication habits, 1912 Laue reaction, career setbacks, Giessen laboratory, Munich chair), Dam (tin-box darkroom, refusal of portrait, 'I did not think; I investigated', 'I am busy'), Assmus (six weeks alone, exact experimenter making own apparatus, cathode rays outside his usual work, Munich theoretical-physics institute), Monville/Dondelinger (15 Jan. 1896 letter: sent the prints himself). EPISODE USE (no episode supports more than two rows): Nov.-Dec. 1895 solitary verification and Boveri remark (Glasser, Assmus) -> analytical_rigor, deep_focus; control-by-photography statement and negative results in the first communication (self) -> analytical_rigor; second-communication delay 'free from criticism' (self) -> analytical_rigor, perfectionism; Zehnder letter Jan. 1896 'facts are the important thing' (Glasser) -> analytical_rigor; Dam interview quotes on verifying before publishing (Dam) -> analytical_rigor; 'four weeks' without experiments and refusal of lecture invitations 1896 (Glasser) -> deep_focus, social_assertiveness; Utrecht call declined 1888 (Glasser) -> deep_focus; Dam 'I am busy' (Dam) -> deep_focus; wife's letter 4 March 1896 (Glasser) -> deep_focus; Hertz letter 1888 and unpublished/re-edited results (Glasser) -> perfectionism; small-effect measurements with Kundt (Glasser, Assmus) -> detail_orientation; white-lead door strips (Röntgen's lecture as reported by Glasser) -> detail_orientation; Nobel lecture declined, 1905 congress refused, portrait refused (Glasser, Dam) -> social_assertiveness; habitual solitary work, Kohlrausch letter, co-authorships (Glasser, Monville, Nobel note) -> collaboration; research range and the 1894-95 turn to cathode rays (Glasser, Assmus, Dam) -> curiosity; longitudinal-to-transverse view (Barker preface) and the 1912 Laue photographs (Glasser) -> belief_updating; tin-box darkroom, homemade air thermometer, self-built apparatus (Dam, Glasser, Assmus, Nobel note) -> resourcefulness; Utrecht expulsion, failed examination, Zurich route, Privatdozent block (Glasser, Nobel note, Assmus) -> persistence; Zurich application, Giessen laboratory, Munich theoretical-physics institute (Glasser, Assmus) -> proactive_agency; AEG/patent reply and Nobel prize donation (Glasser, memorial) -> impact_motivation. ROWS CONSIDERED AND LEFT UNSCORED: autonomy_need (solitary habits and declined offers overlap collaboration/deep_focus; he worked contentedly inside state institutes -- omitted); conflict_tolerance (Kundt clash, Lenard dispute, 'let the envious chatter in peace' versus 'these lies affect me a great deal more than they should', 'gruff and even rude' -- mixed characterisations, omitted); mastery_orientation (student torchlight-parade speech and rectorial address are self statements of motive -- not scored); experimentation (systematic testing is rigour rather than novelty-seeking; omitted); independent_thinking (refusal to adopt speculative hypotheses folded into analytical_rigor); leadership_drive (rectorship and directorships are offices; omitted); achievement_drive, competitiveness, execution_speed (published seven weeks after the discovery but otherwise slow to publish -- mixed), decisiveness, risk_tolerance (Glasser's 'fear of disrepute' is his speculation), ambiguity_tolerance, discipline, planning_orientation, adaptability, systems_abstraction, intuitive_synthesis, creative_originality, cross_domain_range, aesthetic_sensitivity, persuasiveness, opportunity_sensing -- insufficient on-point evidence. EXCLUDED ON PURPOSE: his wife's illness and death, his own illnesses and cause of death, eye condition and colour-blindness, childlessness and the adoption of his niece (and Glasser's remarks on how he raised her), his mother's death, wartime rationing and the inflation loss of his savings, loneliness in old age -- read in Glasser and the Nobel note, NOT used for anything; his political remarks of 1918-1923 and wartime honours (zero-politics); hunting, mountaineering and the 'simplified x-rays' parlour trick (leisure). The refusal of personal nobility attached to the Bavarian Order of Merit (1896) is reported only by Glasser (chronology and ch. IX); it was not independently verified and is used in no row or editorial item. The Lenard priority dispute is read as context only; no claim is made about who first produced X-rays, and no 'father of radiology' or 'first' claim is made beyond the first Nobel Prize in Physics. KNOWN LIMITS: the main biographical source (Glasser) is an admiring commemorative volume and is the only route to Röntgen's letters, since his will ordered his scientific and personal correspondence burned (Glasser) -- so private working habits are thinly evidenced; Dam's interview contains biographical errors (birthplace near Zurich, degree at Utrecht); Assmus says Röntgen 'delivered the news' on 28 Dec. 1895, when the manuscript was submitted rather than read. Confidence is kept at or below 0.70 and scores below 85 throughout.
